newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-ROMANCE AND NOSTALGIA PROVIDE HEART OF ASHES MYSTIQUE.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-ROMANCE AND NOSTALGIA PROVIDE HEART OF ASHES MYSTIQUE.

text.p: Romance and nostalgia provide the heart of the Ashes mystique which will again captivate millions when battle resumes between Australia and England this Thursday.
Personalities have flourished since the colonial upstarts defeated their imperial masters in 1882, inspiring a mock obituary to English cricket in the Sporting Times.

Later that year Ivo Bligh took a team to Australia, promising to bring back "the Ashes of English cricket". He fulfilled his goal and in Melbourne was presented by two ladies with the small urn which has since remained at Lord's.
Some time this week, Shane Warne will amble to the crease for his opening delivery of the series, reviving instant memories of his first ball against the old enemy four years ago.
As Mike Gatting watched with bemused incredulity, the ball pitched outside the leg stump and spun wickedly to hit the top of the off-stump. The series was effectively won with a single delivery.
Warne is the latest and quite possibly the greatest in the distinguished line of Australian leg-spinners who learned their craft on sun-baked pitches responding only to speed or wrist spin.

Arthur Mailey floated profligate leg spin in the 1920s, Clarrie Grimmett bowled in the same decade and again in the 1930s with miserly control while the fiery Irishman Bill O'Reilly delivered medium pace wrist spin with the aggression of a fast bowler.
Watching intently throughout this summer's six-test series and delivering laconic television commentary will be Richie Benaud, a sinuous spinner, dashing batsman and inspirational captain.
The opening salvo will not be fired by Warne, but possibly by the lean and menacing Glenn McGrath, a thoroughbred among fast bowlers.
Since "The Demon" Fred Spofforth scythed through the England batting in the last 19th century, the great Australian teams have featured great pace bowlers.

The best of all was probably Dennis Lillee, featuring a moustache as imposing as the growth sported by Spofforth a century earlier, and possessing a similar command of the mechanics of propelling a cricket ball at speed.
Then there was Ray Lindwall, cutting edge of the imperious Australian sides immediately after World War Two and a model of rhythm and power.

Lindwall hunted in tandem with Keith Miller, the most glamorous cricketer to grace a cricket field, while Lillee was assisted by Jeff Thomson, a pure force of nature and maybe the fastest of all time.
Raw speed, a concept refined by West Indies during their period of world domination in the 1980s, usually wins series.

Harold Larwood destroyed Australia and reduced their sporting idol Don Bradman to the rank of a mere mortal in the bodyline series of 1932-33, Frank Tyson ruined several careers in 1954-55 and John Snow was instrumental in winning back the Ashes in 1970-71.
Bob Willis took Mike Brearley's side to victory in 1977 and, more famously, routed Australia at Headingley in 1981.
Opposing McGrath will be England captain Mike Atherton, chewing gum and looking warily around the field after taking guard.
Atherton, who knows another series defeat against the old enemy means the end of his tenure as England captain, thrives under pressure.

In the 1920s, Jack Hobbs produced his best on the most difficult pitches with the opposition at their fiercest. So do did Len Hutton, in the 1940s and early 1950s when he defied Lindwall and Miller and also Geoff Boycott who played his first test against Australia in 1964 and was still opening the batting 17 years later.
At the heart of Australia's batting order this year stands Steve Waugh, as tough a competitor as any in the history of the Ashes.
Waugh has methodically refined his game to eliminate error, has a particular liking for English bowling and averages 50 in test cricket, the accepted benchmark separating the great from the good.
Ranked number one in the world by both the leading English cricket magazines, Waugh's average is still just fractionally over half the astounding 99.94 recorded by Bradman.
Bradman is one of the handful of sportsmen who transcend their game and no history of Australia during the depression of the 1930s would be complete without an account of his life.
Sport humbles as well as raises its exponents and Bradman's final innings for his wonderful 1948 side has become part of cricket mythology.
Needing four runs to average 100 in test cricket and score 7,000 runs, Bradman was bowled second ball by Eric Hollies for a duck.

"I wonder," said John Arlott, commentating on the radio, "if you see the ball very clearly in your last test in England, on a ground where you've played some of the biggest cricket of your life and where the opposing side has just stood around you and given you three cheers and the crowd has clapped you all the way to the wicket.
"I wonder if you really see the ball at all?"
